questions.q: What does combining GovernorTimelockControl with Governor require, in terms of overrides?
options: Six explicit override functions, resolving functions both parent contracts declare
No overrides at all -- the contract compiles with no extra code
Only a single override of the constructor
A full rewrite of the Governor base contract itself
questions.explain: The lesson lists six required overrides (state, proposalNeedsQueuing, _queueOperations, _executeOperations, _cancel, _executor) needed to resolve the shared declarations.

questions.q: In the deployment order this lesson teaches, why must the token be deployed before the Governor?
options: The Governor's constructor needs the deployed token's address to read voting power from
Solidity requires contracts to be deployed in alphabetical order
The token must be deployed last for security reasons
There is no required order -- any order works identically
questions.explain: The lesson explains the order matters because each contract needs an address from a contract deployed before it, and the Governor's constructor takes the token's IVotes address.

questions.q: What is the final step in the deployment sequence, and why does it matter?
options: Renouncing the deployer's TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE, which finishes the handoff to on-chain governance
Minting additional governance tokens to the deployer
Deleting the Governor contract's source code
Setting the voting period to zero
questions.explain: The lesson calls renouncing the admin role the step that finishes the handoff -- without it the deployer retains a standing backdoor.

questions.q: In the proposal lifecycle, what must happen before a Queued proposal can move to Executed?
options: The timelock's mandatory delay must fully elapse
A second, separate vote must be held
The Governor contract must be redeployed
All token holders must individually approve execution
questions.explain: The lesson's lifecycle table states Executed only happens once the timelock delay has elapsed after Queued.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a proposal's free-text description is not what actually gets voted on?
options: Because what executes is the array of target addresses, values, and calldata passed into propose() -- the description is just a string
Because Governor contracts ignore all proposal descriptions entirely
Because descriptions are stored off-chain and never recorded
Because voters vote on the proposer's reputation, not any content
questions.explain: The lesson's key principle is that a trustworthy proposal UI decodes and displays the actual calls, since the description could in theory not match what the contract will really execute.
